newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan March import car sales jump ahead of tax.
newsitem.headline: Japan March import car sales jump ahead of tax.

text.p: Japan's sales of imported vehicles jumped in March because of strong demand ahead of an increase in the national sales tax, according to figures released on Friday.
But the gains went mainly to European producers, with U.S. carmakers seeing a slump in sales.

The Japan Automobile Importers Association (JAIA) said sales of imported vehicles rose 12.7 percent in March from a year earlier to 57,840 units, surpassing the previous March record of 51,342 marked last year.
Japan raised the consumption tax to five percent on Tuesday from the previous three percent.

For the fiscal year to the end of March, imported vehicle sales rose 8.8 percent to a record 437,886 units. This was 7.9 percent of overall domestic vehicle sales in 1996/97, a rise of 0.1 percentage point from the previous year.
Most European carmakers such as Volkswagen, Mercedes-Benz, BMW, Adam Opel, Peugeot, and Volvo saw their highest sales ever for March, JAIA said.
German sales rose 41.1 percent from a year earlier to 29,831, British sales rose 83.4 percent to 5,340, Swedish car sales rose 11.6 percent to 3,055 and French sales rose 43.4 percent to 1,772.
But sales of U.S.-made vehicles fell 34.8 percent to 11,830, due mainly to poor sales of Ford and Japanese maker's U.S.-made cars.

"Japanese consumers' taste is shifting to compact cars so that bulky American cars and off-road type cars are likely to become out-of-date here," the trade body's vice-chief secretary, Kunihiko Ono, said.
Such large vehicles have been popular here in recent years.

A recent survey by the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association said Japanese demand for compact cars was expected to rise due to an increase in buying by women and elderly people, who prefer small cars that are easy to manoeuvre.
Ono said he saw a five percent rise in sales for 1997 but that most of the gains have already happened because of buying before the sales tax increase.

"A huge drop in June sales is likely. Dealers usually expect good sales in June and July because bonuses are paid to Japanese workers in those months. But this year, many consumers may have purchased cars in March ahead of the sales tax, in expectation of the bonus payment," Ono said.
Some European automakers, including Volkswagen and Mercedes-Benz, are also offering low-rate financing to boost sales while BMW has cut prices for a limited time to draw in potential buyers.
